name: Lip competence training

lead: Lip competence training means keeping the lips gently sealed at rest, a habit oral-posture communities practice for better jaw and facial development and a more closed, composed look.

In orthodontics, lip competence is a clinical descriptor meaning the lips close at rest without strain. A sealed-lip position is also a core element of mewing, alongside tongue posture, lightly touching teeth and nasal breathing. No reviewed study tests whether training lip closure changes facial structure.

paras: Practitioners close the lips softly, breathe through the nose and hold the position through the day as part of a routine with tongue posture. Some use mouth taping at night to encourage closure.
Reference sources say mouth taping used to encourage lip closure carries risks and needs professional supervision.

angle.text: Oral-posture communities practice resting with sealed lips, saying it guides jaw growth and supports facial development. It is done as an everyday habit alongside nasal breathing and tongue posture. Lip competence is an orthodontic descriptor, and no study tests training it.

lead: Lip competence training is the habit of keeping the lips gently sealed at rest, with the teeth lightly together and breathing through the nose. People who practise it say a consistent lip seal supports a balanced lower face, a defined jawline and a less strained, more relaxed look around the mouth and chin, and it is usually practised as one part of a wider oral-posture routine. [1]

In orthodontics, lip competence is a clinical descriptor meaning the lips can close at rest without strain, and lip incompetence means they cannot. Clinical writing links lip incompetence with certain bite patterns and lower-face proportions and describes restoring a spontaneous lip seal as a treatment goal. [2][3]

A sealed-lip position is a core element of mewing, which is associated with the orthodontists John Mew and his son Mike Mew and their practice of orthotropics. [4][5] Published studies have recorded lip competence as a feature of the face, and a controlled clinical trial in myofunctional therapy has examined lip strength and lip sealing in patients, but no study found has tested lip-closure training as a way to change facial structure in people without a bite problem. [2][6][7]
infobox: Lip competence: lips close at rest without strain [2]
Mouth taping to encourage closure during sleep

paras: Practice guidance in mewing descriptions is to close the lips softly while breathing through the nose.  A looksmax.org series on mewing describes the basic idea as lips together, teeth together and tongue on the roof of the mouth, and says the lip seal should become subconscious. Its author suggests checking on waking for a dry mouth or sore jaw muscles as signs of night-time mouth breathing, and says that recruiting extra muscle such as the mentalis to force the lips shut is undesirable. [1]
Some practitioners use mouth taping to encourage lip closure during sleep, which a reference article says carries risks and needs professional supervision.

In dentistry and oral surgery, lip competence is a recorded feature of the face. A 1977 report on surgical-orthodontic correction of skeletal open bite lists lip incompetence among indications for the procedure and lip competence among contraindications for a particular type of case. [2] A population study of incisor trauma in adolescents tested lip coverage among its occlusal risk factors. [6]

A 1991 French review of labial incompetence describes lips that fail to meet at rest as an anomaly bound up with jaw growth, lip function and facial form, with a vertical imbalance in the lower third of the face and a disorder of orofacial muscle behaviour. Its stated treatment aim is to restore a spontaneous lip seal, using functional orthopaedic appliances early in growth, orthodontics in adolescents and adults, and surgery where jaw or tissue problems require it. [3]

Orofacial myofunctional therapy (MFT), a field of exercises for the muscles around the mouth, has also studied lip function: a controlled clinical trial published in the International Journal of Orofacial Myology examined the relationship of lip strength and lip sealing in MFT. [7] A paper on clinical estimation of mouth breathing in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics addresses how clinicians assess a related habit. [8] A Cochrane review of treatments for anterior open bite in children, a bite pattern whose causes include oral habits and mouth breathing, noted that the interventions are not supported by strong scientific evidence. [9]

sections.h: Lip seal in orofacial myofunctional therapy
paras: Outside the looksmaxxing context, lip-seal exercises belong to orofacial myofunctional therapy, which trains the muscles of the lips, tongue and face. A controlled clinical trial published in the International Journal of Orofacial Myology enrolled 91 patients who had barely acquired lip sealing and compared a group that did lip button-pull exercises with a group that did not. Lip strength did not differ between groups at the first examination; in the button-pull group it roughly doubled after six months and then declined, and 25 percent achieved complete lip sealing, 41 percent incomplete sealing and 31 percent no change.[7]

A Cochrane review of treatments for anterior open bite in children identified three randomised trials. A Frankel function regulator (FR-4) appliance combined with lip-seal training corrected open bite compared with no treatment (risk ratio 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.38), as did a palatal crib with high-pull chincup; the reviewers rated the evidence for both as weak, with potential bias, and not sufficient to guide clinical practice.[9] These trials concern children with a diagnosed bite problem, not cosmetic lip-seal practice in healthy adults.

Mewing is named after John Mew, a British orthodontist (1928 to 2025) who developed orthotropics with his son Mike. Wikipedia reports that Mew proposed in 1958 that malocclusion was a postural deformity, argued that the tongue resting against the palate widens the upper jaw, and summarised the DIY version as standing up straight and shutting the mouth.[4] Google Trends interest in mewing began rising in January 2019, and it spread widely on social media, especially in looksmaxxing communities.[5]

The American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, and a 2019 review in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery found inadequate evidence that it works or can replace orthognathic surgery.[4][5] Mike Mew was struck from the UK dental register in 2024 after a misconduct process; the General Dental Council had earlier reprimanded John Mew in 2010 and revoked his registration in 2017 over advertising and confidentiality matters, while the NHS case against him in the 1980s ended with a 1987 High Court appeal he won.[4][5]

Orthotropics proponents hold that a closed mouth and correct oral posture guide growth. [4] Lip seal is the element of this routine that is most easily described and observed, which is why it shows up in beginner guides.

No studies found that test lip competence training as an intervention for facial appearance in healthy people. Clinical literature records lip competence as a feature associated with bite type and dental trauma risk [2][6]; a controlled trial in orofacial myofunctional therapy examined lip strength and lip sealing in 91 patients [7]; and a Cochrane review includes lip-seal training with an appliance in children with open bite, rating the evidence weak [9]. None evaluates a lip-seal training programme for facial change. 2025 pilot studies of orofacial myofunctional therapy reported effects on hyoid position and jaw pain but did not directly test mewing or lip sealing.

Lip seal appears in forum guides as a daily habit paired with tongue posture and nasal breathing. [1] Another looksmax.org thread discusses a surgical route to proper lip seal, a Le Fort I osteotomy that moves the upper jaw forward, which shows how some posters connect lip competence with jaw position. [10]

lore.intro: Lip seal is discussed alongside tongue posture and nasal breathing as part of an overall posture routine, and some posters connect it with jaw surgery. [1][10]

claims.claim: Keeping the lips sealed at rest improves jaw and facial development.
A face with a long lower third makes lips hard to seal, and people strain the chin to compensate.
Mouth breathing at night leaves the mouth open and can be checked on waking.
Jaw surgery can give a proper lip seal.

timeline.event: John Mew proposes malocclusion as a postural deformity, the seed of orthotropics.[4]
Surgical-orthodontic open-bite report lists lip incompetence as an indication. [2]
French review describes restoring spontaneous lip seal as the aim in labial incompetence. [3]
Interest in mewing, which includes lip seal, begins rising. [5]
Mike Mew struck from the UK dental register.[5]
